# Beyond the Context Window: Architecting Long-Form Story Generation

![Sujith Reddy](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:64:64/1*jHC8VBE9yqBMBYQntQdyHg.jpeg)

7 min read

Feb 25, 2026

--

At Pratilipi, we deal in stories that never end.

Unlike a typical novel with a compact arc, web-serialized fiction is episodic, high-stakes, and massive in scale. A single story can run for thousands of chapters over years. It needs recurring cliffhangers, evolving character arcs, and enough continuity that readers don’t feel cheated.

When we set out to build an AI-assisted story generation pipeline, we hit a hard truth:

LLMs can write strong scenes. They struggle to sustain a saga.

Ask an LLM to “write a story” and it tends to wrap everything up in a neat few hundred words. Ask it to “write Chapter 50 of an ongoing thriller,” and it may invent missing history, forget motivations, or resurrect characters who died earlier.

We learned that long-form generation isn’t primarily a prompting problem. It’s a systems engineering problem. We had to stop treating stories as streams of tokens and start treating them as stateful systems with constraints, contracts, and memory.

Note: This approach works for stories with minimal / generic world-building and non-critical locations, where the narrative is primarily driven by character conflict and plot progression.It tends to break on complex world-building, non-linear structures, and stories with heavy long-range foreshadowing.It’s not a universal solution, but the learnings are worth sharing.
